## Introduction {#sec-intro}

Our body temperature, hormone secretion, and waves of sleepiness follow cycles of approximately 24 hours. Similar rhythms of roughly one day occur in the opening and closing of plant leaves, the formation of fungal spores, and even in single-celled bacteria. They are called *circadian rhythms*, from Latin words meaning "about a day."

Not every fluctuation with a period of roughly 24 hours qualifies as a circadian rhythm, however. Circadian rhythms are known to have three main properties. First, they continue to oscillate with a period of about 24 hours even under constant light and temperature conditions: *self-sustained oscillation*. In other words, organisms do not merely trace the external day–night cycle passively; they carry a clock of their own inside the body. Second, they can shift the hands of that clock, its phase, to align with cycles of light and darkness or temperature: *entrainment*. Because an internal clock's period is not exactly 24 hours, it must be reset a little every day. Third, its period changes very little when the ambient temperature changes: *temperature compensation*.

Of these three properties, temperature compensation is the most puzzling. In general, chemical reaction rates depend strongly on temperature: many biological reactions become about two to three times faster for a 10 °C rise. This factor is called the temperature coefficient, Q~10~. An internal clock, too, must run through a succession of chemical reactions, such as protein binding and phosphorylation. We might therefore expect it to run faster on warm days and slower on cold ones. Yet the period Q~10~ of actual circadian rhythms generally lies between about 0.8 and 1.2.^[In this article, the period Q~10~ is defined as $\tau(T)/\tau(T+10\,^\circ\mathrm{C})$. It exceeds 1 when warming shortens the period, or speeds up the clock, so its direction agrees with the Q~10~ of an ordinary chemical reaction. Some publications use the reciprocal, $\tau(T+10\,^\circ\mathrm{C})/\tau(T)$ [@fu2024], so care is needed when comparing values.] The individual components are temperature-sensitive, yet the clock as a whole, assembled from them, is not.

This property also seems somewhat at odds with the second property, entrainment. To entrain to a temperature cycle, a clock must be able to sense changes in temperature. To achieve temperature compensation, on the other hand, it must be insensitive to temperature. How, then, can a clock sense temperature and yet not be governed by it? We will return to this question in the second half of the article.

Cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, hold a special place in approaching this puzzle. They are photosynthetic bacteria. In 1993, experiments using a bioluminescent reporter showed that their gene expression exhibits a circadian rhythm with a temperature-compensated period [@kondo1993]. At the heart of this clock are three proteins: KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC.

Even more remarkably, in 2005, simply mixing these three proteins with ATP in a test tube was shown to produce a self-sustained oscillation in the phosphorylation state of KaiC with a period of approximately one day [@nakajima2005]. The periods were approximately 22, 21, and 20 hours at 25, 30, and 35 °C, respectively, giving a Q~10~ of about 1.1. In a test tube with no gene transcription or translation, and not even a cell, a temperature-compensated clock was keeping accurate time.

If temperature compensation occurs with only three kinds of protein in a test tube, we can pursue its mechanism thoroughly, through both molecules and mathematics. This article approaches the question from a systems biology perspective: understanding the clock's properties through the behavior of an interconnected reaction network as a whole, rather than through the properties of individual molecules alone. We first review the basic workings of the KaiABC clock and formulate the conditions for temperature compensation mathematically. We then run a mathematical model of the actual clock in Python to see what those equations mean in practice. Looking beyond the period to how the size of the oscillation (its amplitude) and its phase change with temperature, we then sort the ways in which a clock unaffected by temperature can still sense it into three types, and compare them with experimental data and with measured temperature dependences of individual reactions. All code in the article can be run as written to reproduce the figures.

## How the KaiABC oscillator works {#sec-kai}

The central player, KaiC, is a ring-shaped protein made of six subunits: a hexamer. Each subunit contains two domains, CI and CII. Together, the six subunits form two stacked rings, one of CI domains and one of CII domains, in a barrel-like shape roughly 10 nm in both height and width (@fig-kaic (a)) [@pattanayek2004; @egli2013]. Both domains bind ATP. The hexamer binds 12 ATP molecules in total, each nestled at an interface between neighboring subunits.

KaiC can both phosphorylate and dephosphorylate itself. Phosphorylation occurs at two sites in the CII domain: serine 431 (S431) and threonine 432 (T432). Each KaiC subunit can therefore occupy four states in total: U, with neither site phosphorylated; T, with only T432 phosphorylated; ST, with both sites phosphorylated; and S, with only S431 phosphorylated. During oscillations in vitro, these states follow a fixed order. T432 is phosphorylated first, producing T, followed by S431, producing ST. The phosphate on T432 is then removed, producing S, and finally the phosphate on S431 is removed, returning the subunit to its original U state [@nishiwaki2007; @rust2007].

Panel (b) of @fig-kaic shows the CII ring sliced at the height of S431 and T432 and viewed from above. The two phosphorylation sites, shown in magenta, face the subunit interfaces and lie right next to ATP molecules, shown in yellow, bound to neighboring subunits. The phosphate group is thought to be transferred across the subunit interface from the neighboring ATP [@egli2013].

KaiA and KaiB drive this directional cycle. KaiA binds to KaiC and stimulates its autophosphorylation. While KaiA is active, KaiC is phosphorylated step by step, from U to T and then ST. Eventually, however, dephosphorylation sets in and S accumulates; KaiB then binds to S-state KaiC, and the resulting complex in turn sequesters KaiA, preventing it from acting [@rust2007]. Deprived of KaiA's help, KaiC proceeds in the dephosphorylation direction, from ST through S and then to U. As S declines, the sequestered KaiA is released, and phosphorylation begins again. As phosphorylation proceeds, S builds up, and S itself then shuts down phosphorylation. It is this delayed negative feedback that generates the self-sustained oscillation (@fig-cycle).

KaiC has another property essential to understanding temperature compensation. It is also an ATP-hydrolyzing enzyme, or ATPase, but an extraordinarily slow one. Each KaiC subunit hydrolyzes a mere 15 or so ATP molecules per day, and this ATPase activity is itself temperature-compensated [@terauchi2007]. The left panel of @fig-atpase plots ATPase activity from 25 to 35 °C. Its Q~10~ is approximately 1.0 for KaiC alone and stays at about 1.2 even with KaiA and KaiB added, behaving clearly differently from a typical chemical reaction (Q~10~ = 2, dashed line). Furthermore, measurements across KaiC mutants with different periods showed that ATPase activity was neatly proportional to the frequency of their in vivo rhythms, the reciprocal of the period (@fig-atpase, right). In other words, the higher (faster) the ATPase activity of a KaiC, the faster its clock runs.

Why is this activity so slow and so insensitive to temperature? An atomic-level structural study of the CI domain identified two main causes of the slow rate: the water molecule used for hydrolysis is held in an unfavorable position for the reaction, and ATP hydrolysis is coupled to peptide-bond isomerization with a high activation energy [@abe2015]. The same study reported that ATPase activity shortly after adding ATP to KaiC alone, within the first two hours, was temperature-dependent (Q~10~ ≈ 1.4), whereas steady-state activity after at least 24 hours was almost temperature-independent (Q~10~ ≈ 1.1). Furthermore, substituting just a single amino acid in KaiC can change the period dramatically, anywhere from 15 to 158 hours. Moreover, temperature compensation remains largely intact in many of these period mutants [@itomiwa2020].

The connection between ATPase activity and period has also been tested against changes in temperature. In KaiC mutants whose ATPase activity lost temperature compensation, compensation of the phosphorylation rhythm's frequency broke down in the same direction [@furuike2022]. In three mutants with ATPase Q~10~ values elevated to 1.5–1.7, frequency Q~10~ values also rose, to 1.2–1.6. In a mutant whose ATPase instead slowed down as temperature increased (Q~10~ ≈ 0.5), frequency also decreased with temperature (Q~10~ ≈ 0.7). In addition, spontaneous dissociation of the KaiB–KaiC complex in the absence of KaiA is also very slow and, again, temperature-compensated in its own right (Q~10~ ≈ 1.05) [@simon2022]. Several of the gears that make up the clock are themselves insensitive to temperature.

These observations might suggest that the secret of temperature compensation lies entirely in the properties of a single component, KaiC. But the fact that the ATPase on its own is temperature-compensated does not guarantee that the period of the whole clock is compensated as well. Many temperature-sensitive reactions exist both within and outside KaiC, and we need to understand how the overall period is determined when they are connected as a network. More fundamentally, what mathematical condition does "the period is independent of temperature" correspond to in a system of many reactions? The next section begins by writing this condition down as equations.

## Expressing temperature compensation mathematically {#sec-math}

### Temperature dependence of reactions

The temperature dependence of a chemical reaction's rate constant $k$ is often well described by the Arrhenius equation:

$$
k(T) = A \exp\left(-\frac{E}{RT}\right)
$$ {#eq-arrhenius}

Here, $T$ is absolute temperature, $R$ is the gas constant, $E$ is the activation energy, and $A$ is the pre-exponential (frequency) factor, a constant with little temperature dependence. Think of the activation energy as the height of an energy barrier that the reaction must cross. The higher the barrier, the more strongly the reaction accelerates when temperature rises.

From @eq-arrhenius, the ratio of reaction rates when temperature rises from $T$ to $T + 10$ K, namely the reaction's Q~10~, is given by

$$
\ln Q_{10} = \frac{E}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T+10}\right) \approx \frac{10\,E}{RT^{2}}
$$ {#eq-q10}

For example, a reaction with an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol becomes approximately 1.9 times faster when warmed from 25 to 35 °C. @fig-q10 shows the relationship between activation energy and Q~10~. ### Period control coefficients

The clock's period $\tau$ depends on the rate constants $k_1, k_2, \dots, k_n$ of many reactions in the network. We quantify the influence of each rate constant on the period by

$$
C_i = \frac{\partial \ln \tau}{\partial \ln k_i}
$$ {#eq-cc}

$C_i$ is a dimensionless quantity giving the percentage change in period caused by a 1% change in the rate constant of reaction $i$, and is called a *period control coefficient*. It applies to the period of an oscillation the idea of *metabolic control analysis*, which quantifies how strongly each enzyme in a metabolic network controls the overall flow of reactions, or flux [@ruoff2003]. If $C_i$ is negative, accelerating that reaction shortens the period; this is the more intuitive case. If $C_i$ is positive, on the other hand, accelerating it instead lengthens the period.

Control coefficients have a simple but extremely important property. Suppose we accelerate all reaction rate constants at once by the same factor $\lambda$. This is equivalent to watching the clock in fast-forward at $\lambda$ times normal speed. Neither the order of reactions nor the waveforms traced by the concentrations of each state change; only the time axis shrinks by a factor of $1/\lambda$. The period therefore becomes exactly $1/\lambda$ times as long:

$$
\tau(\lambda k_1, \dots, \lambda k_n) = \frac{\tau(k_1, \dots, k_n)}{\lambda}
$$

Taking logarithms of both sides, differentiating with respect to $\ln\lambda$, and setting $\lambda = 1$ gives

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i = -1
$$ {#eq-sum}

This is called the *summation theorem*. Here, "all reactions" means all rate constants whose units contain inverse time (such as $\mathrm{h}^{-1}$). Parameters with concentration units, such as binding dissociation constants, and quantities such as total protein concentrations do not change when we fast-forward time, so they are excluded from this sum.

### The condition for temperature compensation

We now have everything we need. When temperature changes, each rate constant changes according to @eq-arrhenius, and its effect on the period is transmitted through its control coefficient. Applying the chain rule and substituting $d\ln k_i/dT = E_i/RT^2$, we can write the temperature dependence of the period as

$$
\frac{d \ln \tau}{d T} = \sum_{i} \frac{\partial \ln \tau}{\partial \ln k_i}\,\frac{d \ln k_i}{d T} = \frac{1}{RT^{2}} \sum_{i} C_i E_i
$$ {#eq-dlntau}

For the period to be independent of temperature, therefore, the sum on the right must vanish:

$$
\sum_{i} C_i E_i \approx 0
$$ {#eq-tc}

This is the condition for temperature compensation [@ruoff2003; @ruoff2005]. It can be understood as a "ledger": enter the temperature effect of each reaction on the period as "control coefficient × activation energy," and balance the entries so that their total is zero.

What follows when we combine this ledger equation with the summation theorem (@eq-sum)? If every reaction has the same activation energy $E$, then $\sum_i C_i E_i = E\sum_i C_i = -E$, and the clock's period shortens as temperature rises, exactly as it would for a single chemical reaction with activation energy $E$. In other words, however complex the reaction network may be, complexity alone cannot produce temperature compensation. Because activation energies are generally positive, canceling the contributions of reactions with negative control coefficients (reactions that shorten the period when accelerated) requires reactions with positive control coefficients: reactions that, when accelerated, instead lengthen the period. Their activation energies must also be sufficiently large. In a clock with many temperature-sensitive reactions, temperature compensation thus rests on a delicate balance in which period-shortening and period-lengthening reactions cancel each other's responses to temperature.

This conclusion rests on two assumptions. The first is that every reaction accelerates as temperature rises: its activation energy is positive. If we allow temperature-dependent equilibrium constants, discussed in the next subsection, or composite processes with negative apparent activation energies, positive entries in the ledger can arise in other ways. The second is that the activation energy of each reaction is appreciably greater than zero. If all activation energies were nearly zero, the period would not change with temperature to begin with, even without period-lengthening reactions. The "uniformly insensitive" strategy discussed in Section 7, and the view that KaiC ATPase activity is itself temperature-compensated, are closer to this position. The idea of explaining temperature compensation through cancellation between reactions, on the other hand, has long been proposed as the *balance hypothesis* [@ruoff1992]. More recently, the conditions under which period-lengthening reactions arise have been investigated in detail as a general theory of biochemical oscillators [@fu2024].

### Contributions from equilibrium constants

Finally, there is one more type of term to consider: processes such as molecular binding and dissociation that are described by equilibrium constants rather than rate constants. The temperature dependence of an equilibrium constant $K$ follows the van 't Hoff equation,

$$
\frac{d \ln K}{d T} = \frac{\Delta H}{R T^{2}}
$$

where $\Delta H$ is the standard reaction enthalpy change. If $C_K$ is the period control coefficient for $K$, then @eq-dlntau acquires a term $C_K\,\Delta H$:

$$
\frac{d \ln \tau}{d T} = \frac{1}{RT^{2}}\left(\sum_i C_i E_i + \sum_j C_{K_j} \Delta H_j\right)
$$ {#eq-dlntau-full}

Unlike activation energies, $\Delta H$ can be either positive or negative. Temperature-induced shifts in binding equilibria can therefore provide another way to balance the period ledger. In the model used here, the constant $K_{1/2}$ governing KaiA's effect enters in this way.

@eq-tc tells us what is required for temperature compensation to hold. But looking at an abstract equation alone cannot reveal which reactions in the actual KaiABC clock shorten the period and which lengthen it. To find out, we need to actually run a concrete mathematical model of the clock.

## Running a KaiABC model {#sec-model}

We now turn to a mathematical model of the KaiABC clock and run it in Python. We use the model proposed by Rust and colleagues in 2007 [@rust2007]. They measured, transition by transition, how fast KaiC moves between its phosphorylation states, both with and without KaiA. They then showed that simply combining these experimentally determined rate constants was sufficient to reproduce the in vitro phosphorylation rhythm fairly well. The model has only three variables, yet captures the essence of the KaiABC clock well. It does not, however, explicitly include the KaiC ATPase reaction step. The rate constants in the model are "effective rate constants" that lump together various elementary processes, including ATP hydrolysis. This point will become important when we consider the role of ATPase in the second half of the article.

### Model equations

The variables are the concentrations $T$, $D$, and $S$ of KaiC in the T, ST, and S states. We use $D$ for ST, from *doubly phosphorylated*. The U-state concentration follows by subtracting the other three from the total KaiC concentration: $U = [\mathrm{KaiC}] - T - D - S$. All transitions between the four states are written as first-order reactions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dT}{dt} &= k_{UT}\,U + k_{DT}\,D - (k_{TU} + k_{TD})\,T \\
\frac{dD}{dt} &= k_{TD}\,T + k_{SD}\,S - (k_{DT} + k_{DS})\,D \\
\frac{dS}{dt} &= k_{US}\,U + k_{DS}\,D - (k_{SU} + k_{SD})\,S
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-rust}

Here, $k_{XY}$ is the rate constant for the transition from state X to state Y. Besides the four arrows drawn in @fig-cycle, the equations include reverse transitions, such as dephosphorylation from T to U.

Feedback enters because these rate constants depend on the concentration of KaiA that is free to act. As we saw in Section 2, S-state KaiC sequesters and inactivates KaiA together with KaiB. The original paper assumes that each S-state KaiC subunit sequesters one KaiA dimer, or two KaiA molecules counted as monomers, and writes the free KaiA concentration $A$ as

$$
A = \max\{0,\ [\mathrm{KaiA}] - 2S\}
$$ {#eq-freeA}

The KaiB concentration does not appear explicitly in the equations. KaiB is assumed to be sufficiently abundant and to bind instantly to S-state KaiC, so its effect is folded into @eq-freeA. Each rate constant then depends on the free KaiA concentration $A$ in a Michaelis–Menten (hyperbolic) form:

$$
k_{XY} = k^{0}_{XY} + k^{A}_{XY}\,\frac{A}{K_{1/2} + A}
$$ {#eq-kxy}

Here, $k^0_{XY}$ is the rate constant in the absence of KaiA, $k^A_{XY}$ is the increase in rate at maximal KaiA stimulation, and $K_{1/2}$ is the KaiA concentration at which its effect is half-maximal.

In this article, we use a slightly rearranged version of @eq-kxy to make the later analysis easier to follow. Because $f = A/(K_{1/2} + A)$ can be interpreted as "the fraction of KaiC bound to KaiA," we can write

$$
k_{XY} = (1 - f)\,k^{\mathrm{free}}_{XY} + f\,k^{\mathrm{bound}}_{XY},
\qquad k^{\mathrm{free}}_{XY} = k^{0}_{XY},\quad k^{\mathrm{bound}}_{XY} = k^{0}_{XY} + k^{A}_{XY}
$$ {#eq-kxy2}

In other words, the effective rate constant $k_{XY}$ is expressed as a weighted average of the rate for KaiA-free KaiC, $k^{\mathrm{free}}_{XY}$, and the rate for KaiA-bound KaiC, $k^{\mathrm{bound}}_{XY}$. Organized this way, each constant becomes a pure rate constant describing "how fast KaiC in a particular state changes," making it easier to apply the Arrhenius equation in the next section.

@tbl-params lists the parameter values from the original paper's supplementary material, converted to this form. Note that the KaiA-bound ST → S and S → U rate constants calculated from the original values come out slightly negative. Under the conditions used in this article (KaiA = 1.3 µM), the bound fraction $f$ never exceeds approximately 75%, so even with the original values the overall reaction rate $k_{XY}$ never becomes negative. From the next section onward, however, we apply the Arrhenius equation to individual rate constants, and negative rate constants cannot be handled. We therefore set these two values to zero. Let us now implement this model in code. The functions accept arrays of parameters so that many parameter sets can be simulated at once later on.

::: {#model .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
R_GAS = 8.314e-3                     # Gas constant (kJ / mol / K)
KAIA, KAIC, KHALF = 1.3, 3.4, 0.43   # Concentrations (µM)

# Nine nonzero rate constants (1/h): _b for KaiA-bound, _f for KaiA-free
RATES0 = {"UT_b": 0.479077, "TD_b": 0.212923, "SD_b": 0.505692, "US_b": 0.0532308,
          "TU_b": 0.21 + 0.0798462, "DT_b": 0.173,
          "TU_f": 0.21, "DS_f": 0.31, "SU_f": 0.11}
RATE_NAMES = list(RATES0)
LABELS = {"UT_b": "U→T (KaiA)", "TD_b": "T→ST (KaiA)", "SD_b": "S→ST (KaiA)",
          "US_b": "U→S (KaiA)", "TU_b": "T→U (KaiA)", "DT_b": "ST→T (KaiA)",
          "TU_f": "T→U (no KaiA)", "DS_f": "ST→S (no KaiA)", "SU_f": "S→U (no KaiA)"}

def base_params():
    return {**RATES0, "KHALF": KHALF, "KAIA": KAIA, "KAIC": KAIC}

def rhs(x, P):
    """Right-hand side of eq-rust. Array x has shape (3, N) for N parameter sets."""
    T, D, S = x
    U = P["KAIC"] - T - D - S
    A = np.maximum(0.0, P["KAIA"] - 2.0 * S)          # Free KaiA
    f = A / (P["KHALF"] + A)                          # Fraction bound to KaiA
    g = 1.0 - f
    kUT, kTD, kSD, kUS = f * P["UT_b"], f * P["TD_b"], f * P["SD_b"], f * P["US_b"]
    kTU = f * P["TU_b"] + g * P["TU_f"]
    kDT = f * P["DT_b"]
    kDS, kSU = g * P["DS_f"], g * P["SU_f"]
    dT = kUT * U + kDT * D - (kTU + kTD) * T
    dD = kTD * T + kSD * S - (kDT + kDS) * D
    dS = kUS * U + kDS * D - (kSU + kSD) * S
    return np.array([dT, dD, dS])
```
:::


We integrate the differential equations numerically using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method (RK4). Following the original paper, the initial concentrations are 0.68 µM T, 1.36 µM ST, and 0.34 µM S. After allowing enough time for the oscillations to settle onto a steady orbit, we measure the period from the times at which the total amount of phosphorylated KaiC, $T + D + S$, crosses its time average from below. Crossing times are found by linear interpolation, and the period is the mean interval between successive crossings.

::: {#integrator .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Numerical integration and period measurement"}
X0 = np.array([0.68, 1.36, 0.34])

def stack(params_list):
    """Convert a list of parameter dictionaries to a dictionary of arrays."""
    return {k: np.array([p[k] for p in params_list], float) for k in params_list[0]}

def integrate(P, t_end, dt=0.01, x0=None, record_every=10, forcing=None):
    """Integrate N parameter sets with RK4; forcing(t) returns parameters at time t."""
    N = np.size(P["KAIC"])
    x = np.tile(X0.reshape(3, 1), (1, N)) if x0 is None else np.array(x0, float).reshape(3, -1)
    ts, ys = [], []
    for i in range(int(round(t_end / dt))):
        t = i * dt
        if i % record_every == 0:
            ts.append(t); ys.append(x.copy())
        P1, P2, P3 = (forcing(t), forcing(t + dt / 2), forcing(t + dt)) if forcing else (P, P, P)
        k1 = rhs(x, P1); k2 = rhs(x + 0.5 * dt * k1, P2)
        k3 = rhs(x + 0.5 * dt * k2, P2); k4 = rhs(x + dt * k3, P3)
        x = x + dt / 6.0 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)
    return np.array(ts), np.array(ys)          # ys has shape (time, 3, N)

def crossing_times(t, P):
    """Upward crossings of the mean of P, found by linear interpolation."""
    c = P - P.mean()
    i = np.where((c[:-1] < 0) & (c[1:] >= 0))[0]
    return t[i] - c[i] * (t[i + 1] - t[i]) / (c[i + 1] - c[i])

def period_amp_from(t, y, t_skip):
    """Period and amplitude (peak-to-trough T+D+S) for each parameter set; NaN and 0 if nonoscillatory."""
    m = t >= t_skip
    Ptot = y[m].sum(axis=1)
    half = len(Ptot) // 2
    per = np.full(Ptot.shape[1], np.nan)
    amp = np.zeros(Ptot.shape[1])
    for j in range(Ptot.shape[1]):
        a1, a2 = np.ptp(Ptot[:half, j]), np.ptp(Ptot[half:, j])
        if a2 < 1e-3 or a2 < 0.95 * a1:                   # No oscillation, or still decaying
            continue
        d = np.diff(crossing_times(t[m], Ptot[:, j]))
        if len(d) >= 2 and d.std() / d.mean() < 0.02:   # Count only regular oscillations
            per[j] = d.mean()
            amp[j] = np.ptp(Ptot[:, j])
    return per, amp

def period_amp(params_list, t_end=900.0, t_skip=500.0, dt=0.01):
    t, y = integrate(stack(params_list), t_end, dt)
    return period_amp_from(t, y, t_skip)
```

## Introducing temperature {#sec-naive}

To build temperature changes into the model, we give each of the nine rate constants in @tbl-params a temperature dependence using the Arrhenius equation (@eq-arrhenius). Taking the reference temperature $T_0$ to be 30 °C and requiring the rate constants to equal the values in @tbl-params there, the rate constant at temperature $T$ becomes

$$
k_i(T) = k_i(T_0)\,\exp\left[-\frac{E_i}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T_0}\right)\right]
$$ {#eq-arrhenius-ref}

Because $K_{1/2}$ is an equilibrium constant, we use the van 't Hoff equation when assigning its temperature dependence. Expressed as a deviation from the reference temperature, it has exactly the same functional form.

::: {#at-temperature .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
T_REF = 30.0   # Reference temperature (°C)

def at_temperature(p, temp_c, E, H=0.0):
    """Parameters at temp_c (°C). E maps rate constants to activation energies (kJ/mol);
    H is the enthalpy change for K_1/2 (kJ/mol)."""
    T, T0 = temp_c + 273.15, T_REF + 273.15
    factor = lambda e: np.exp(-(e / R_GAS) * (1.0 / T - 1.0 / T0))
    q = dict(p)
    for n in RATE_NAMES:
        q[n] = p[n] * factor(E[n])
    q["KHALF"] = p["KHALF"] * factor(H)
    return q
```
:::

## Dissecting compensation through sensitivity analysis {#sec-sensitivity}

### Calculating control coefficients numerically

The period control coefficients in @eq-cc are easy to calculate numerically. We increase and decrease each rate constant slightly, one at a time (here by ±1% on a logarithmic scale), measure the period, and estimate the partial derivative from the difference (the central difference method).

::: {#control-coeffs .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def control_coeffs(p, names, h=0.01):
    """Estimate C = d ln(period) / d ln(parameter) by central differences."""
    plist = []
    for n in names:
        for s in (+1, -1):
            q = dict(p)
            q[n] = p[n] * np.exp(s * h)
            plist.append(q)
    per, _ = period_amp(plist)
    return {n: (np.log(per[2 * i]) - np.log(per[2 * i + 1])) / (2 * h) for i, n in enumerate(names)}

C_all = control_coeffs(p0, RATE_NAMES + ["KHALF", "KAIA", "KAIC"])
C = {n: C_all[n] for n in RATE_NAMES}
Cv = np.array([C[n] for n in RATE_NAMES])
C_sum = Cv.sum()
```

The great majority of reactions have negative control coefficients, as intuition suggests. Of these, dephosphorylation from ST to S without KaiA shortens the period most strongly, with a coefficient of \-1\.17. S → ST in particular has a control coefficient of about +1: accelerating it lengthens the period by nearly the same proportion. In Section 3, we argued that temperature compensation requires "reactions that lengthen the period when accelerated." In this model, S → ST is precisely a reaction that can play that role.

### Why does S → ST lengthen the period?

The S → ST reaction pushes S-state KaiC back into the ST state. As discussed in Section 2, S acts as a brake: together with KaiB, it sequesters KaiA and stops phosphorylation. If S → ST is fast, S is slow to accumulate, and it takes longer for all the KaiA to be sequestered. Phosphorylation advances further during this time, driving more KaiC into phosphorylated states. Returning all of them to their original states during the subsequent dephosphorylation phase then takes longer as well. As a result, both the phosphorylation and dephosphorylation phases lengthen.

Temperature compensation rarely arises by chance when activation energies are chosen at random. Building a temperature-compensated clock requires specific relationships among the activation energies of the reactions. How, then, are these relationships realized? And how do differences in the way the ledger is balanced change the clock's properties, such as whether it runs stably across a broad temperature range and how well it withstands mutations?

## Ways to balance the period ledger {#sec-strategies}

There is more than one way to balance the period ledger (@eq-tc) to zero. We begin by comparing two balancing strategies that are opposite in character. Both are models that reduce an idea to an extremely simple form, so many of the comparison's results follow from those premises themselves. We nevertheless start with these two extremes because they show clearly how dramatically the way the ledger is balanced changes the clock's behavior. More realistic strategies lying between the two are considered in Section 9.

The first strategy keeps every activation energy small. Each term $C_i E_i$ is then small to begin with, so the ledger as a whole cannot tilt much. As discussed in Section 2, KaiC ATPase activity and the spontaneous dissociation of the KaiB–KaiC complex are themselves temperature-compensated [@terauchi2007; @simon2022]. The idea is that "if every gear of the clock is insensitive to temperature, the whole clock will be too." Here, we call a clock with all activation energies except that of S → ST set to 10 kJ/mol, corresponding to a reaction-rate Q~10~ of about 1.1, the *uniformly insensitive strategy*. Note, however, that this is an extreme reduction of that idea to its simplest form, not the hypothesis that "KaiC ATPase determines the period" itself. What that hypothesis claims is that "the main rate-limiting reactions that set the period are temperature-compensated"; it does not go so far as to require every reaction in the network to be temperature-insensitive. This distinction becomes important in Section 9.

The second strategy gives every reaction an activation energy typical of ordinary chemical reactions (50 kJ/mol, corresponding to Q~10~ ≈ 1.9), while making the activation energy of the period-lengthening S → ST reaction especially large so that large negative and large positive entries cancel. The idea that temperature compensation results from balancing reactions with opposing thermal effects dates back to Hastings and Sweeney [@hastings1957]; Ruoff later extended it to general reaction network models [@ruoff1992]. Here, we call the model that directly embodies this balance hypothesis the *cancellation strategy*.

In both strategies, we set the activation energy of S → ST so that the period ledger $\sum_i C_i E_i$ is exactly zero at 30 °C.

::: {#strategies .cell execution_count=21}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def balance_E(E_base, E_sensor=None):
    """Set activation energies other than S→ST to E_base; override U→T if E_sensor is given.
    Choose S→ST to balance the period ledger at 30 °C."""
    E = {n: E_base for n in RATE_NAMES}
    if E_sensor is not None:
        E["UT_b"] = E_sensor
    E["SD_b"] = -sum(C[n] * E[n] for n in RATE_NAMES if n != "SD_b") / C["SD_b"]
    return E

STRATEGIES = {"A": balance_E(10.0), "B": balance_E(50.0)}
NAMES = {"A": "A: Insensitive", "B": "B: Cancellation", "C": "C: Coupled", "R": "R: Division of labor"}
COLORS = {"A": BLUE, "B": ORANGE, "C": "#a3401a", "R": AQUA}

def q10_rate(E):
    """Rate Q10 from 25 to 35 °C for a reaction with activation energy E (kJ/mol)."""
    return np.exp(E / R_GAS * (1 / 298.15 - 1 / 308.15))
```

Running stably over a broad temperature range and robust to mutations—judging from the comparison so far, the uniformly insensitive strategy seems to make a far better clock. But as noted in Section 1, a circadian clock has another important property besides "not being governed by temperature": "sensing temperature."

## A clock must sense temperature {#sec-sensing}

Two experimental facts show that the real clock keenly senses temperature: "the clock stops when cooled," and "the clock entrains to temperature cycles."

### The clock stops at low temperature

Being temperature-compensated does not mean that the clock keeps running at any low temperature. Murayama and colleagues gradually cooled the in vitro KaiABC clock and examined its behavior in detail [@murayama2017]. As temperature fell, only the amplitude decreased markedly while the period stayed almost unchanged, until self-sustained oscillations disappeared at approximately 19 °C. Below that temperature, the behavior switched to "damped oscillations," in which an external perturbation elicits oscillations that gradually decay. Single-cell observations have shown that clocks in living cells also stop at low temperature through the same type of bifurcation [@mihalcescu2025]. In fact, this behavior had been predicted theoretically before the experiments. In the mathematical model of Hatakeyama and Kaneko, in which temperature compensation arises because multiple phosphorylation states compete for a limited amount of KaiA, cooling was shown to reduce the amplitude and eventually eliminate oscillation through a Hopf bifurcation [@hatakeyama2012].

In general, there are two representative types of bifurcation through which an oscillation disappears (or appears). In one, the amplitude gradually shrinks to zero while the period remains at a finite value: a *Hopf bifurcation*. In the other, the amplitude is retained while the period diverges to infinity: a *SNIC bifurcation*, or saddle-node bifurcation on an invariant circle. The experimental finding that only the amplitude vanishes while the period stays almost constant clearly indicates that the clock stops through a Hopf bifurcation.

### A Hopf bifurcation in the model

Looking back at @fig-strategies-temp in Section 7, the cancellation strategy stopped oscillating on the cold side. Let us investigate the mechanism mathematically.

When oscillation stops, the concentrations of the phosphorylation states no longer change with time: the system sits at a *steady state* (fixed point) of the differential equations. A small displacement from that state evolves as $e^{\lambda t}$, where $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of the Jacobian at the steady state. If the real parts of all eigenvalues are negative, the displacement decays and the steady state is stable; if any eigenvalue has a positive real part, the displacement is amplified and oscillation emerges. A Hopf bifurcation is the critical point at which the real parts of a complex-conjugate pair of eigenvalues with nonzero imaginary parts change sign from negative to positive as a parameter such as temperature varies. The period of the small oscillation emerging just beyond the bifurcation can be predicted from the imaginary part as $2\pi / |\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda|$.

::: {#hopf .cell execution_count=28}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from scipy.optimize import fsolve

def f1(x, q):
    return rhs(np.asarray(x).reshape(3, 1), q).ravel()

def jacobian(x, q, h=1e-7):
    J = np.zeros((3, 3))
    f0 = f1(x, q)
    for j in range(3):
        xx = np.array(x, float); xx[j] += h
        J[:, j] = (f1(xx, q) - f0) / h
    return J

def fixed_point(q):
    x = fsolve(lambda x: f1(x, q), [0.8, 0.45, 0.57], xtol=1e-13)
    assert np.linalg.norm(f1(x, q)) < 1e-9
    return x

E_B = STRATEGIES["B"]
T_grid = np.round(np.arange(21.0, 30.01, 0.25), 2)
lam = []
for T in T_grid:
    q = at_temperature(p0, T, E_B)
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(jacobian(fixed_point(q), q))
    lam.append(ev[np.argmax(ev.real)])
lam = np.array(lam)
T_c = np.interp(0.0, lam.real, T_grid)          # Temperature at which the real part crosses zero

# Amplitude and period just above the bifurcation (integrate longer because convergence is slow)

per_fine, amp_fine = period_amp([at_temperature(p0, T, E_B) for T in T_fine],
                                t_end=8000, t_skip=7000, dt=0.02)
```

### Can the clock entrain to temperature cycles?

In Section 1, we noted that "temperature compensation and entrainment seem to contradict each other." To entrain to a temperature cycle, a clock must sense changes in temperature. Can clocks built on our two temperature-compensated strategies, then, entrain well to an externally imposed temperature cycle?

Whether a clock can entrain to a temperature cycle depends strongly on the difference between the clock's own period (its natural period) and the period of the temperature cycle. From this point on, we therefore multiply all model rate constants by the same factor so that the natural period at 30 °C matches the value measured in vitro by Yoshida and colleagues, 23.1 hours [@yoshida2009], before making comparisons. This merely rescales the time axis, so it does not affect the discussion of temperature dependence. We then vary the temperature as a sine wave centered on 30 °C, with an amplitude of ±ΔT and a period of 24 hours, and examine whether the clock's period is pulled into (locked to) 24 hours.

``` {.python .cell-code}
def run_forced(p, E_rows, temp_fun, t_end=2400.0, t_skip=1400.0):
    """Integrate N parameter sets with time-varying temperature; return each set's mean period and variation.
    E_rows contains (N, 9) activation energies; temp_fun(t) returns an array of temperatures (°C) for the sets."""
    E_rows = np.asarray(E_rows, float)
    N = len(E_rows)
    base = {k: np.full(N, v) for k, v in p.items()}
    T0K = T_REF + 273.15
    def params_at(t):
        TK = temp_fun(t) + 273.15
        fac = np.exp(-(E_rows / R_GAS) * (1.0 / TK[:, None] - 1.0 / T0K))
        q = dict(base)
        for i, n in enumerate(RATE_NAMES):
            q[n] = p[n] * fac[:, i]
        return q
    t, y = integrate(base, t_end, dt=0.01, forcing=params_at, record_every=10)
    m = t >= t_skip
    Ptot = y[m].sum(axis=1)
    stats = []
    for j in range(N):
        d = np.diff(crossing_times(t[m], Ptot[:, j]))
        stats.append((d.mean(), d.std()) if len(d) >= 3 else (np.nan, np.nan))
    return np.array(stats), t, y

def is_locked(stat, T_cycle):
    return abs(stat[0] - T_cycle) < 0.05 and stat[1] < 0.05

def sine_entrainment(keys, dTs=(1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0), t_end=3000.0, t_skip=2000.0):
    members = [(k, dT) for k in keys for dT in dTs]
    amp_arr = np.array([dT for _, dT in members])
    stats, t, y = run_forced(p_ref, [[STRATEGIES[k][n] for n in RATE_NAMES] for k, _ in members],
                             lambda t: 30.0 + amp_arr * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 24.0), t_end, t_skip)
    min_lock = {k: min([dT for (kk, dT), s in zip(members, stats) if kk == k and is_locked(s, 24.0)],
                       default=np.nan) for k in keys}
    return min_lock, members, t, y
```

The cancellation strategy locks to 24 hours under a temperature cycle as small as ±1 °C, with peaks arriving at the same time each day. The uniformly insensitive strategy, however, does not entrain until the temperature swing is increased to ±5 °C (in @fig-entrain, the peaks of the blue curve drift a little further each day under the ±2 °C temperature cycle). Theoretically, even temperature-compensated clocks have been shown to entrain to temperature cycles whose period is close to their natural period [@bodenstein2012]. In practice, however, the more insensitive a clock's individual reactions are to temperature, the harder it is to pull into a temperature cycle.

Why, then, can a clock entrain to temperature cycles even though its period is temperature-compensated? @fig-limitcycles overlays the limit cycles at 28 and 32 °C. In the uniformly insensitive strategy, the limit cycles at the two temperatures nearly coincide. In the cancellation strategy, by contrast, the size and position of the limit cycle change substantially with temperature, even though the time needed to complete a cycle (the period) is almost the same. As a result, when the temperature switches partway through a cycle, the clock's state at that moment is left off "the limit cycle of the new temperature" and is then drawn toward the new orbit. Its phase shifts during this process. "The period does not change with temperature, but the orbit traced by the clock does move with temperature"—this is one reason temperature compensation and entrainment can coexist. In a recent preprint, which has not yet undergone peer review, Liu and colleagues likewise cite earlier work [@yoshida2009; @francois2012] and characterize "the temperature-dependent change in the size and position of the limit cycle while the period remains nearly constant" as precisely what enables phase shifts in response to temperature changes [@liu2026]. Moreover, several clock models, including a KaiC model, show that the very mechanism compensating the period deforms the limit cycle, which in turn produces phase shifts, so that "period robustness and phase plasticity are two sides of the same coin" [@hatakeyama2015]. Deformation of the orbit is not the only mechanism for a phase shift, however. Even if the orbit's shape itself is unchanged, a temperature-induced change in the distribution of speed along the orbit—which parts are traversed quickly and which slowly—will shift the phase when temperature changes. Other work has shown that such waveform distortions affect both temperature compensation and the range of entrainment [@gibo2025]. François and colleagues further point out that in a clock whose period is compensated by balancing many reactions, the mean levels of its constituent proteins vary with temperature, so the shape of the limit cycle should vary with temperature as well [@francois2012].

## Ledgers for amplitude and phase response {#sec-amplitude}

### Amplitude control coefficients

Many indicators describe the shape of a limit cycle. Here we take as representative the amplitude $A$, defined as the peak-to-trough difference in the total amount of phosphorylated KaiC, $T+ST+S$. Exactly as for the period, we define the amplitude control coefficient $C^A_i$ as

$$
C^{A}_i = \frac{\partial \ln A}{\partial \ln k_i}
$$ {#eq-cca}

This measures the fractional change in amplitude caused by a fractional change in a rate constant.

Amplitude control coefficients also obey a summation theorem. Accelerating all rate constants by the same factor, we saw, is the same as fast-forwarding time. Fast-forwarding does not change the range over which the concentration of each phosphorylation state rises and falls; only the time scale changes. The amplitude is therefore unchanged, and the following summation theorem holds:

$$
\sum_i C^{A}_i = 0
$$ {#eq-sum-a}

Whereas the right-hand side of the period summation theorem (@eq-sum) was $-1$, the right-hand side of the amplitude summation theorem is $0$. Both are fundamental relations already derived in metabolic control analysis of oscillatory phenomena [@kholodenko1997].

The change in amplitude with temperature can also be written in the same form as the period equation (@eq-dlntau):

$$
\frac{d \ln A}{d T} = \frac{1}{RT^{2}} \sum_i C^{A}_i E_i
$$ {#eq-dlnA}

If the period ledger $\sum_i C_i E_i$ is zero, the period does not change with temperature. If, on the other hand, the amplitude ledger $\sum_i C^A_i E_i$ is nonzero, the amplitude changes with temperature. The two ledgers are separate equations, so it should be possible to keep one balanced at zero while leaving the other strongly tilted.

The amplitude summation theorem yields another important property as well. Using @eq-sum-a, we can rewrite the amplitude ledger in terms of deviations from the mean activation energy $\bar{E}$:

$$
\sum_i C^{A}_i E_i = \sum_i C^{A}_i \left(E_i - \bar{E}\right)
$$ {#eq-amp-dev}

(Because $\sum_i C^A_i = 0$, this equality holds for any constant in place of $\bar{E}$, not just the mean. What essentially matters is how strongly the activation energies $E_i$ and the amplitude control coefficients $C^A_i$ correlate across reactions.) If every reaction had the same activation energy, the right-hand side would be zero and the amplitude would not change with temperature at all. For amplitude to increase as temperature rises, activation energies must vary across reactions, and moreover there must be a tendency for "reactions that increase the amplitude ($C^A_i > 0$) to have larger activation energies." In other words, the experimental fact that "the amplitude of a temperature-compensated clock changes with temperature" is itself evidence that the activation energies of the reactions making up the clock are not uniform.

This argument, however, assumes that temperature changes only rate constants. If equilibrium constants such as $K_{1/2}$ also vary with temperature, their contributions enter the amplitude ledger as well. Stated more precisely, then, "if amplitude changes with temperature, the effect of temperature is more than a uniform fast-forwarding of the whole clock." What the observed change in amplitude directly rules out is this assumption of "uniform fast-forwarding." It does not go so far as to rule out mechanisms centered on temperature-insensitive reactions themselves. As we will see shortly, even when the differences in activation energy between reactions are small, the amplitude can change greatly with temperature if the clock's operating point is close to a bifurcation.

Indeed, quantities that change with temperature are known in temperature-compensated circadian clocks across many organisms: the expression level of the clock protein FRQ in *Neurospora crassa* [@liu1998], the amplitude of expression rhythms of some clock genes in cultured rat cells [@kurosawa2017], and the amplitude of the phosphorylation rhythm in the KaiABC clock [@murayama2017] each change with temperature. Theory has also long predicted that the amplitude of temperature-compensated oscillators increases as temperature rises [@ruoff2003]. Here, we place this alongside the period ledger and evaluate it quantitatively in the language of control coefficients.

In Murayama and colleagues' data, the amplitude increases by approximately 9% per °C between 25 and 30 °C; converted to a ledger value using @eq-dlnA, this corresponds to about 65 kJ/mol. In other words, the real clock's amplitude ledger is tilted strongly positive. In terms of @eq-amp-dev, this means that the reactions that increase the amplitude have activation energies well above the mean.

One caution applies to this experimental estimate, however. In Murayama and colleagues' data, the squared amplitude $A^2$ decreases almost linearly with temperature in the low-temperature range. This is exactly the $A \propto \sqrt{T - T_c}$ behavior expected near a Hopf bifurcation, in which case $d\ln A/dT = 1/\{2(T - T_c)\}$, so the slope of the log-derivative grows divergently as the bifurcation point $T_c$ is approached. A linear regression of the squared amplitude on the data at or below 26 °C estimates the bifurcation point $T_c$ at approximately 19\.9 °C, and converting $1/\{2(T - T_c)\}$ at the intermediate temperature of 27.5 °C into ledger units (kJ/mol) gives approximately 50 kJ/mol. The large amplitude ledger calculated from the experimental data is thus also a sign that the 25–30 °C range still lies within the sphere of influence of the Hopf bifurcation.

### The phase-response ledger

The amplitude ledger tells us how the size of the oscillation changes with temperature and whether oscillation tends to stop at low temperature. But it is not the amplitude that directly determines whether the clock can entrain to an external temperature cycle. What does is the *phase response*: how far the clock's phase advances (or is delayed) when the temperature changes slightly. Even if the amplitude changes with temperature, entrainment to a temperature cycle does not occur if the clock advances by the same amount no matter at which phase the temperature is changed.

Let us therefore write $g_i(\phi)$ for how much the speed at which the phase advances changes when the rate constant of reaction $i$ is changed slightly, for a clock at phase $\phi$ (with one cycle represented by $0 \sim 2\pi$); it is the change in phase velocity per change in the logarithm of the rate constant. Raising temperature by $\delta T$ changes each log rate constant by $E_i\,\delta T / RT^2$, so the clock's phase response (phase sensitivity) to a change in temperature, $\Gamma_T(\phi)$, can be written as

$$
\Gamma_T(\phi) = \frac{1}{RT^{2}} \sum_i E_i\, g_i(\phi)
$$ {#eq-gamma}

This, too, is a ledger of the same form as those for the period and amplitude, but now it is a "ledger of functions" that takes a value at each phase $\phi$.

Here, again, the "fast-forwarding time" argument applies. Increasing every rate constant by the same factor simply moves the clock around the same orbit faster by that factor, so the phase velocity increases by the same proportion at every phase. Thus, $\sum_i g_i(\phi)$ is independent of the phase $\phi$ and equals the clock's angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi/\tau$. Also, the average of $g_i(\phi)$ over one cycle equals $-\omega C_i$, because it is precisely the change in the time per cycle caused by changing that rate constant. This relationship, in which integrating the phase response over one cycle yields the period sensitivity, is well known in oscillator sensitivity analysis [@gunawan2006; @taylor2008]. Using these two properties, @eq-gamma can be decomposed as

$$
\Gamma_T(\phi) = -\frac{\omega}{RT^{2}} \sum_i C_i E_i + \frac{1}{RT^{2}} \sum_i \left(E_i - \bar{E}\right)\left(g_i(\phi) + \omega C_i\right)
$$ {#eq-gamma-split}

The first term on the right is the period ledger itself, a constant independent of phase. If the period is temperature-compensated, this first term is zero. The only part that varies with the phase $\phi$ is therefore the second term, and it is determined solely by the deviations $E_i - \bar{E}$ from the mean activation energy.

This leads to one clear conclusion: **if the effect of temperature is merely to fast-forward time, the clock can never entrain to temperature cycles.** A temperature change then only alters the clock's rate of advance by the same proportion at every phase, generating no force that brings the clock's hands into line at a particular phase. A clock in which all reactions have equal activation energies (for example, the all-50-kJ/mol clock in Section 5) is exactly such a case. As with amplitude, however, what this conclusion rules out is only the assumption that "the effect of temperature is solely a uniform fast-forwarding." In a clock whose period is temperature-compensated yet which shows some response to temperature, activation energies necessarily vary from reaction to reaction. What really matters, therefore, is not whether they vary, but "which reactions are assigned which temperature dependences."

Let us now calculate each reaction's phase response $g_i(\phi)$ numerically. At each phase of the oscillation, we change one rate constant slightly for a short interval (30 minutes) and measure the phase shift after sufficient time has passed.

::: {#prc .cell execution_count=35}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def phase_response(p, names, n_phase=64, eps=0.05, pulse=0.5):
    """Perturb each parameter by exp(±eps) for a duration pulse at each phase, and use the phase shift to estimate
    the reaction's phase response g_i(φ): change in phase velocity per unit ln k_i, in 1/h."""
    t, y = integrate(stack([p]), 1600, dt=0.01, record_every=1)
    Ptot = y[:, :, 0].sum(axis=1)
    keep = t > 1200
    level = Ptot[keep].mean()
    def up_cross(tt, PP):
        c = PP - level
        i = np.where((c[:-1] < 0) & (c[1:] >= 0))[0]
        return tt[i] - c[i] * (tt[i + 1] - tt[i]) / (c[i + 1] - c[i])
    tc = up_cross(t[keep], Ptot[keep])
    tau = np.diff(tc).mean()
    i0 = np.searchsorted(t, tc[0])                        # Phase 0: T+ST+S crosses its mean from below
    starts = [i0 + int(round(j * tau / n_phase / 0.01)) for j in range(n_phase)]
    cols = [(j, None, 0) for j in range(n_phase)] + \
           [(j, n, s) for j in range(n_phase) for n in names for s in (+1, -1)]
    base = {k: np.full(len(cols), v) for k, v in p.items()}
    pert = {k: v.copy() for k, v in base.items()}
    for c, (j, n, s) in enumerate(cols):
        if n is not None:
            pert[n][c] *= np.exp(s * eps)
    x0 = np.concatenate([y[starts[j], :, 0].reshape(3, 1) for j, _, _ in cols], axis=1)
    tt, yy = integrate(base, 6 * tau, dt=0.01, x0=x0, record_every=2,
                       forcing=lambda s: pert if s < pulse else base)
    PP = yy.sum(axis=1)
    first = []
    for c in range(len(cols)):
        cc = up_cross(tt, PP[:, c])
        first.append(cc[cc > 4 * tau][0])                 # First crossing after sufficient relaxation
    first = np.array(first)
    pos = {col: k for k, col in enumerate(cols)}
    wrap = lambda d: (d + tau / 2) % tau - tau / 2
    g = {}
    for n in names:
        adv = [wrap(first[pos[(j, None, 0)]] - first[pos[(j, n, +1)]])
               - wrap(first[pos[(j, None, 0)]] - first[pos[(j, n, -1)]]) for j in range(n_phase)]
        g[n] = np.array(adv) * (2 * np.pi / tau) / (2 * eps * pulse)
    return np.arange(n_phase) / n_phase * 2 * np.pi, tau, g

phi_g, tau_g, g_rate = phase_response(p_ref, RATE_NAMES)
omega_g = 2 * np.pi / tau_g
RT2 = R_GAS * (T_REF + 273.15) ** 2
sum_g = sum(g_rate.values()) / omega_g

def gamma_T(E):
    """Temperature phase response Γ_T(φ), per kelvin, in 1/h."""
    return sum(E[n] * g_rate[n] for n in RATE_NAMES) / RT2

def gamma_first_harmonic(E):
    """Magnitude of the fundamental harmonic of Γ_T."""
    G = gamma_T(E)
    return np.hypot(2 * np.mean(G * np.cos(phi_g)), 2 * np.mean(G * np.sin(phi_g)))
```

In any case, in both the amplitude and phase-response ledgers, what essentially matters is the deviation of activation energies from their mean, $E_i - \bar{E}$.

Once the period ledger is balanced, how the amplitude ledger is tilted depends on where in this plot the temperature-sensitive reactions (those with large activation energies) are placed. Broadly, three design strategies can be considered. Note that this is a classification devised for this article to organize our thinking, not established terminology in the field. Actual biological clocks may combine several mechanisms, and how they appear can depend on the level we focus on. For example, if the temperature dependences of several elementary processes within the KaiC molecule cancel to make ATPase activity temperature-insensitive, this is "cancellation" inside the molecule but appears as "a temperature-insensitive component" from the perspective of the clock network as a whole.

The first strategy keeps every reaction temperature-insensitive, as in the uniformly insensitive strategy seen in Section 7. The period and amplitude ledgers both remain close to zero, and the clock barely senses temperature.

The second makes a reaction with positive effects on both period and amplitude, such as S → ST in the upper right, temperature-sensitive. Warming accelerates S → ST, widening the oscillatory excursion and lengthening the period. This offsets the period shortening caused by acceleration of other reactions (for example, ST → S in the lower left). In other words, temperature compensation of the period and the increase in amplitude at high temperature arise simultaneously from the temperature dependence of the same reaction. We call this the *coupled strategy*. The cancellation strategy of Section 7 is an extreme case of the coupled strategy in which every reaction is temperature-sensitive. The view that, in temperature-compensated oscillators, the period is preserved by an increase in amplitude has a long history [@ruoff2003]. One study argued from the analysis of mathematical models that "the period cannot be kept constant unless gene-expression amplitude increases with temperature," and indeed demonstrated increased amplitude for some clock genes in cultured rat cells [@kurosawa2017]. In the KaiABC clock as well, the temperature dependence of the switch mechanism that sets the amplitude has been reported to contribute to period compensation [@liu2026].

The third strategy makes a reaction temperature-sensitive that has almost no effect on period but a strong effect on amplitude, such as U → T straight up in the plot. Increasing the activation energy of such a reaction barely disturbs the period ledger, while tilting only the amplitude ledger strongly. Because the main period-setting reactions remain temperature-insensitive while a separate reaction with no effect on period serves as the temperature sensor, we call this the *division-of-labor strategy*. This idea also has precedents in earlier work. François and colleagues considered oscillator models in which temperature dependence enters only a few terms of the equations, while the remaining core is temperature-independent. In such clocks, changing temperature merely expands or contracts the limit cycle self-similarly, and the shape of the phase-response curve does not depend on temperature either [@francois2012]. Kidd and colleagues developed this further into a "pathway model," in which each period-determining process is individually temperature-compensated and temperature sensing is carried out by a dedicated pathway connected to the clock [@kidd2015].

## Comparing the three strategies with experiments {#sec-experiment}

Which strategy, then, comes closest to the behavior of the actual KaiABC clock? We use the following four experimental facts for comparison:

1. The in vitro rhythm disappears at approximately 19 °C and is undetectable at 18.6 °C or below [@murayama2017].
2. A stable rhythm persists even at a high temperature of 45 °C, with almost the same period as at 30 °C (in the same reaction mixture, 23.4 hours at 30 °C and 23.3 hours at 45 °C). 45 °C was the upper limit of temperatures at which a stable rhythm persisted [@yoshida2009].
3. The period Q~10~ between 25 and 35 °C is approximately 1.05–1.1 [@nakajima2005; @itomiwa2020].
4. The clock entrains to square-wave temperature cycles that alternate between 30 and 45 °C for half a cycle each when their periods are 20–28 hours, but not when they are 16 or 32 hours [@yoshida2009].

Three caveats are needed before comparing the models with experiments. First, measurement conditions and sample states differ slightly from experiment to experiment. Even the period at 30 °C alone ranges from roughly 21 to 26 hours depending on the protein preparation batch and conditions [@nakajima2005; @yoshida2009; @murayama2017]. Period Q~10~ also changes with KaiA concentration: even if it is 1.05 under standard conditions, it rises to 1.27–1.30 when KaiA is increased approximately threefold [@itomiwa2020]. In what follows, we therefore compare periods and amplitudes as ratios (relative values) to their values at 30 °C, focusing on qualitative differences between strategies rather than precise numerical agreement.

Second, some parameters have been adjusted (tuned) to match experimental results. We set the S → ST activation energy in the coupled strategy and the U → T activation energy in the division-of-labor strategy both to 70 kJ/mol, corresponding to a reaction-rate Q~10~ of approximately 2\.5. This value was chosen so that the fourth fact, "the entrainment pattern for 30/45 °C square-wave temperature cycles," agrees with the experimental result (entrainment at 20–28 hours) in both strategies. The entrainment pattern for these temperature cycles therefore cannot itself serve as grounds for distinguishing the coupled and division-of-labor strategies.

Third, the period at 45 °C is not decisive in distinguishing the strategies either. Since every strategy has its period ledger balanced to zero at 30 °C, the period changes relatively little even at 45 °C, as long as oscillation can be sustained on the high-temperature side. The differences between strategies show up most clearly in "the temperature at which oscillation stops on cooling," "the temperature dependence of amplitude," "the ease of entrainment to small sinusoidal temperature cycles," and "robustness to mutations." As in Section 8, the comparison uses a model whose natural period at 30 °C has been rescaled to 23.1 hours.

In @tbl-compare and @fig-vs-exp, the differences between strategies show up most clearly in the temperature at which oscillations stop on cooling. The uniformly insensitive strategy does not stop even when cooled to 10 °C, whereas the cancellation, coupled, and division-of-labor strategies stop oscillating at 24\.5, 24\.5, and 21\.0 °C, respectively. The division-of-labor strategy is closest to the experimental value of about 19 °C, but is still roughly 2 °C too high; in actual experiments, rhythms are still observed at 19.5–21 °C. That said, estimates of the bifurcation point from experimental data also shift somewhat depending on the analysis method. A study that reanalyzed Murayama and colleagues' data from the relaxation responses after temperature steps estimated the bifurcation point at approximately 21.4 °C [@mihalcescu2025]. The difference between the division-of-labor and coupled strategies also shrinks depending on how the parameters are chosen. As shown in Section 9, setting the S → ST activation energy to 50 kJ/mol in the coupled strategy gives a stopping temperature of 21\.5 °C, almost the same as in the division-of-labor strategy. The stopping temperature alone therefore cannot distinguish these two strategies. Note also that the cancellation strategy cannot sustain oscillations up to 45 °C on the high-temperature side; that its period lined up with the 30/45 °C temperature cycle reflects not so much an autonomous oscillator being entrained as the system simply being forcibly shaken by large external temperature changes.

As for the value of the amplitude ledger, none of the strategies reaches the level of approximately 65 kJ/mol estimated from the experimental data. The cancellation strategy comes closest (46 kJ/mol), followed by the division-of-labor strategy (40 kJ/mol) and then the coupled strategy (29 kJ/mol). This ordering does not match the ordering of the temperatures at which oscillation stops on cooling. As cautioned in Section 9, in this model the temperature at which oscillation stops cannot be predicted from the slope given by the amplitude ledger at 30 °C. There is also a shared discrepancy in the shape of the curve along which the amplitude declines (@fig-vs-exp, right). As the bifurcation approaches, all three strategies that stop at low temperature plunge to zero at once from a state that still retains several tens of percent of the 30 °C amplitude (dropping sharply from 47% in the division-of-labor strategy and 64% in the coupled strategy). This is due to the sharp switching effect of KaiA sequestration seen in Section 8. In the experiments, by contrast, the amplitude approached zero gradually toward about 19 °C. In fact, these two discrepancies—"the amplitude ledger falling short of the experimental value" and "the amplitude dropping to zero at once at low temperature"—are not separate problems. As we saw in Section 9, the large experimental value of the amplitude ledger was a sign of the amplitude declining gradually toward the Hopf bifurcation point. In this model, the KaiA-sequestration switch is so sharp that this gradual decline regime barely exists (Section 8). In other words, both discrepancies share the same root cause.

How easily the clock entrains to a sinusoidal temperature cycle with a 24-hour period can be predicted theoretically from the phase response obtained in Section 9. When the clock is driven by a temperature cycle of amplitude $\Delta T$ and angular frequency $\Omega$, the phase difference $\psi$ between clock and temperature cycle obeys, under the approximation of averaging over one cycle, the differential equation

$$
\frac{d\psi}{dt} = (\omega - \Omega) + \Delta T\, H(\psi)
$$ {#eq-locking}

Here, the coupling function $H(\psi)$ is determined by the fundamental harmonic (first Fourier component) of the phase response $\Gamma_T(\phi)$, and its amplitude is half the magnitude of the fundamental, $|\Gamma_1|$. For the phase difference $\psi$ to remain constant (that is, for entrainment), a solution at which the right-hand side vanishes must exist, so the minimum temperature amplitude required for entrainment is predicted to be $\Delta T_{\min} = 2|\omega - \Omega| / |\Gamma_1|$. As @tbl-compare shows, this theoretical prediction agrees well with the results of the numerical simulations. What deserves attention here is that, although the amplitude ledgers of the uniformly insensitive strategy (9 kJ/mol) and the coupled strategy (29 kJ/mol) differ by nearly a factor of three, their ease of entrainment to a sine wave is almost the same (predicted thresholds of ±3\.1 and ±3\.0 °C). To evaluate a clock's capacity for temperature entrainment correctly, we must, after all, look at the "phase-response ledger" rather than the amplitude.

Robustness to mutations divided clearly by strategy. The division-of-labor strategy is as robust as the uniformly insensitive strategy (median $|\ln Q_{10}|$ of 0\.015), while the coupled strategy (0\.028) lies midway between them and the cancellation strategy (0\.052). The coupled strategy also has 10 mutants that lose oscillation at 25 or 35 °C, but since this strategy does not oscillate below 24\.5 °C to begin with, the count also includes the effect of the 25 °C test falling at the edge of its oscillatory range. Note also that no comprehensive experimental data yet exist that would allow a direct comparison of the spread of Q~10~ across a set of mutants.

Keeping $E_0$ fixed at 10 kJ/mol while lowering the U → T activation energy brings the stopping temperature closer to the experimental 19 °C, but the clock then no longer entrains to the temperature cycle with a 28-hour period. Entrainment at a 28-hour period is a marginal phenomenon that appears only once U → T is raised to 70 kJ/mol. If $E_0$ is varied at the same time, on the other hand, it is possible to match both the stopping temperature and the entrainment pattern to experiment. For example, with $E_0$ = 12.5 kJ/mol and U → T = 50 kJ/mol, the stopping temperature is 19\.0 °C and the entrainment pattern is "× ○ ○ ○ ×," both agreeing with the experimental results. This, however, amounts to nothing more than adjusting two free parameters to fit two experimental facts, and does not in itself guarantee that the model is correct.

Conversely, if $E_0$ is increased too far, compensation breaks down on the high-temperature side and the period starts to lengthen. With U → T at 70 kJ/mol, the period at 45 °C remains almost equal to that at 30 °C for $E_0$ up to 15 kJ/mol, but at $E_0$ = 20 kJ/mol it lengthens to 1\.085 times the 30 °C value. An activation energy of 15 kJ/mol corresponds to a reaction-rate Q~10~ of approximately 1\.2. In other words, for the division-of-labor strategy to hold over a broad temperature range, the base reactions that set the period must be about as temperature-insensitive as the KaiC ATPase activity seen in Section 2 (Q~10~ of approximately 1.2 in the presence of KaiA and KaiB) [@terauchi2007]. Whether this premise holds in the actual clock will be examined in the next section using experimentally measured values.

There are several other points of disagreement with experiment. First, the period Q~10~ between 25 and 35 °C is very close to 1.00 in every strategy except the cancellation strategy, so compensation works too well compared with the experimental values (1.05–1.1). This is because the period ledger was balanced exactly to zero at 30 °C. Second, experimentally, stable rhythms are no longer seen above 45 °C, whereas all models except the cancellation strategy keep oscillating beyond 50 °C. This is because the model does not include processes by which proteins denature or lose activity at high temperature. And one more important point: the change in period Q~10~ with KaiA concentration goes in the opposite direction from experiment.

Increasing the KaiA concentration from 1.3 to 1.45 µM in the division-of-labor strategy lowers the period Q~10~ from 1\.003 to 0\.978, moving it in the direction in which warming instead lengthens the period (overcompensation). In actual experiments, however, increasing KaiA has been reported to raise Q~10~ and weaken temperature compensation [@itomiwa2020]. The opposite behavior in the Rust model may be related to its property that increasing KaiA lengthens the period (a positive control coefficient of \+1\.83). To summarize these comparisons: within the Rust model, neither the temperature at which oscillation stops nor temperature entrainment could decisively distinguish the division-of-labor and coupled strategies. Neither strategy, moreover, reproduces the experimental behavior in which the amplitude declines gradually toward low temperature. Even when amplitude and phase response are taken into account in addition to temperature compensation of the period, narrowing the internal design down to one from comparisons of macroscopic phenomena alone is far from easy. And above all, the activation energies used in the calculations so far were all values that we assumed and supplied ourselves.

## Building a ledger from measured values {#sec-measured}

What, then, are the activation energies of the individual reactions in the actual KaiABC clock? In a recent preprint, Liu and colleagues fitted a model to experimental data at 20 °C and at 30 °C separately and estimated the rate constants of the individual KaiC phosphorylation and dephosphorylation steps [@liu2026]. A table in their supplementary material (Table S1) lists, for reactions closely corresponding to those in the Rust model, the ratio of rate constants at 30 versus 20 °C.

The "KaiA-dependent" rates in Liu and colleagues' model correspond to the KaiA-bound rate constants $k^{\mathrm{bound}}$ in @eq-kxy2 of this article, and their "baseline" rates correspond to the unbound $k^{\mathrm{free}}$. The constant describing KaiA's effect corresponds to $K_{1/2}$. However, Liu and colleagues' model is based on the Phong model [@phong2013], an extension of the Rust model, so its reference rate constants differ somewhat from those of the Rust model. The estimated table also includes parameters with large standard errors. For example, the KaiA-bound T → ST and ST → T rates are estimated to fall to less than one fifth when the temperature is raised from 20 to 30 °C, and the standard error of the T → ST rate at 30 °C in particular even exceeds the estimate itself. For this reason, Liu and colleagues themselves selected only five reactions—two well-determined phosphorylation steps and three dephosphorylation steps—and incorporated their temperature dependences into their model. We follow that choice here: we first assign the measured temperature dependences to these five rate constants only and assume the remaining reactions to be temperature-independent. Also, since the temperature dependence of $K_{1/2}$ is not used in Liu and colleagues' model, we compare the cases with and without it side by side.
