Actually running the model with these parameters (@fig-measured-temp) shows, just as the ledger estimate predicts, that the period lengthens dramatically as temperature falls. At 25 °C, the period reaches 2\.4 times the 30 °C value (4\.1 times with $K_{1/2}$ included), and the temperature range over which oscillation is sustained narrows to 23\.5–33\.0 °C. The amplitude ledger is also negative, \-62 kJ/mol, so raising the temperature actually makes the amplitude smaller. Both period and amplitude behave in exactly the opposite way from the actual experimental results. Liu and colleagues themselves likewise report that when only the temperature dependences of the phosphorylation and dephosphorylation rates are included in their model, the period lengthens greatly at low temperature and temperature compensation cannot be reproduced.

In other words, the "large positive term" needed to balance the period ledger is missing entirely. As long as every reaction speeds up as temperature rises (has a positive activation energy), the only reactions that can bring a positive contribution to the ledger are those with positive control coefficients, that is, "reactions that lengthen the period when accelerated." (As noted in Section 3, processes with negative apparent activation energies or changes in equilibrium constants can produce positive contributions in other ways. The reason the ledger deficit shrank when all nine reactions were included earlier is that T → ST, with its negative apparent activation energy, multiplied by a negative control coefficient to produce a positive contribution.) Within the Rust model, the leading reaction with a positive control coefficient is S → ST, but its measured 30 °C / 20 °C rate ratio is small, 1.31 (about 20 kJ/mol), so adding it to the ledger contributes only \+20 kJ/mol.

Liu and colleagues find a candidate for this "missing positive term" outside the Rust model: "the process by which KaiA pulls KaiB off the KaiB–KaiC complex and dissociates it." According to their supplementary material (Table S2), the rate of this reaction increases 3\.49-fold from 20 to 30 °C, corresponding to an activation energy of approximately 92 kJ/mol. Liu and colleagues argue that this very process is a "reaction that lengthens the period when accelerated" in the sense of Fu and colleagues [@liu2026; @fu2024]. Simple division shows that a period control coefficient of roughly 1\.1–1\.3 for this dissociation process would exactly make up the ledger deficit found above (\-105 to \-118 kJ/mol). This simple division, however, is not a mathematically self-consistent estimate. Adding a new reaction to the model redistributes the control coefficients of the existing reactions so that the summation theorem $\sum C_i = -1$ (@eq-sum) is still satisfied. If the newly added reaction has a control coefficient of $+1.2$, for instance, the control coefficients of the remaining reactions must sum to $-2.2$. If that extra negative control coefficient fell on the temperature-sensitive dephosphorylation reactions, the ledger deficit itself would grow further. The values 1.1–1.3 therefore cannot be treated as concrete estimates. All we can say here is that "the sign of the missing term (positive control coefficient × positive activation energy) matches, and its order of magnitude is not absurd." In the Rust model, the dynamics of KaiB–KaiC complex formation and dissociation are compressed into the algebraic relation "S instantly sequesters KaiA" (@eq-freeA), so the contribution of this reaction does not appear in the ledger in the first place. In ledger terms, the reason Liu and colleagues' model reproduced temperature compensation of the period only once temperature dependence was included in the KaiA–KaiB switch mechanism is precisely that this large positive term was then added to the ledger.^[Note that the same Table S2 also estimates that the rate of spontaneous complex dissociation in the absence of KaiA increases 8.8-fold from 20 to 30 °C, indicating strong temperature dependence. This conflicts with Simon and colleagues' direct measurement that complex dissociation in the absence of KaiA is almost temperature-compensated (Q~10~ ≈ 1.05) [@simon2022]. Liu and colleagues themselves cite earlier work in their main text stating that dissociation without KaiA is almost temperature-independent, so individual parameter values obtained by fitting require caution.]

Using this ledger analysis as a guide, the following picture of the actual clock emerges. Temperature-sensitive dephosphorylation reactions (ST → S and S → U) stand on the side that shortens the period, while the equally temperature-sensitive KaiA–KaiB switch mechanism stands on the side that lengthens it, so that a small number of key steps cancel one another in the ledger. Moreover, because that switch mechanism also governs the amplitude of the oscillation [@liu2026], temperature compensation of the period and the increase in amplitude at high temperature arise simultaneously from the same molecular mechanism. In the classification of Section 9, this is a "coupled strategy" concentrated in a few reactions. That said, the strongest support for this picture comes not from our ledger estimate but from the fact that Liu and colleagues, using a mutant that mimics and fixes the phosphorylation state (KaiC-EE), experimentally demonstrated hysteresis (bistability) arising from KaiA–KaiB antagonism, and reproduced temperature compensation in a mathematical model incorporating it. The ledger calculation in this section is best regarded as an auxiliary line for interpreting, from the perspective of control coefficients, what their experiments and model mean.

Also, under this mapping onto the Rust model, the premise of the division-of-labor strategy—that "the main reactions that set the period are all temperature-insensitive"—is incompatible with the measurement that ST → S, which has a large control coefficient, has an activation energy as large as about 71 kJ/mol. A caveat is needed, however: the control coefficients used here are values within the Rust model. Because the Rust model does not explicitly include the KaiC ATPase reaction, control over the period (negative control coefficient) that should really belong to the ATPase may, in the model, be apparently concentrated on ST → S dephosphorylation. Indeed, in the study by Furuike and colleagues introduced in Section 2, the temperature dependence of ATPase activity in mutants was neatly linked to the temperature dependence of the phosphorylation-rhythm frequency [@furuike2022], suggesting that a substantial part of period control in the actual clock lies on the ATPase side. If so, the control coefficient of ST → S in the actual clock would be smaller, and the ledger deficit would not be as large as calculated here.

In short, the discussion here is an inference built on several layers of assumptions. The control coefficients are those of the Rust model, only two temperature points (20 and 30 °C) were measured, and some parameters cannot be determined precisely by fitting the data alone. Moreover, the control coefficient of the crucial switch mechanism cannot be calculated from the Rust model. The reasons the ledger failed to balance include not only reactions missing from the model but also differences in how the model structure distributes control coefficients, differences in how elementary processes are lumped together, and experimental estimation errors. What this mapping establishes with confidence, therefore, is only that "the measured phosphorylation and dephosphorylation rates alone cannot reproduce temperature compensation in the Rust model," that "the sign of the missing term agrees with the properties of the switch mechanism pointed out by Liu and colleagues," and that "this gives strong motivation to test a model that explicitly incorporates the switch mechanism." Even so, it is clear enough that the perspective of "keeping ledgers for the period and amplitude" points concretely to what is missing where in the model, and what should be tested next.

## Discussion: viewing the actual clock through its ledgers {#sec-discussion}

In this article, we have examined strategies for balancing the period ledger by dividing them into three types: "uniformly insensitive," "coupled," and "division of labor." To repeat, this is a framework for organizing our thinking, and the same mechanism may look like a different type depending on the level we focus on. With that in mind, let us organize recent research trends in the language of "ledgers."

First is the view that "the baseline of the period is set by KaiC ATPase." In mutants in which temperature compensation of ATPase activity is broken, temperature compensation of the whole clock's frequency is broken in the same direction [@furuike2022]. For temperature compensation of this ATPase itself, a recent preprint proposes a molecular mechanism [@itomiwa2026]. According to it, the rate-limiting step of the ATPase reaction is ADP release, and as temperature rises, KaiC shifts toward the ADP-bound state, offsetting the acceleration of the hydrolysis reaction. This is "cancellation" inside the KaiC molecule, but from the perspective of the clock's reaction network as a whole, it functions as "a temperature-insensitive component that sets the period." The same preprint further reports that the *amplitude* of the ATPase-activity oscillation depends strongly on temperature (Q~10~ ≈ 2.1). The core component that sets the period is temperature-insensitive, while sensitivity to temperature is carried by the amplitude—in ledger terms, this is a picture close to the "division-of-labor strategy" (as cautioned in Section 7, it differs from the "uniformly insensitive strategy," in which every reaction is temperature-insensitive). The relationship between ATPase activity and the period is not straightforward, however. For example, changing the pH of the reaction mixture has been reported to change the period greatly, from about 15 to 36 hours, while ATPase activity changes by only about 15%, and temperature compensation is preserved [@itomiwa2025]. Also, as we saw in Section 11, the phosphorylation and dephosphorylation steps themselves are temperature-sensitive, so their temperature dependences must cancel somewhere in the network, separately from the ATPase. Furthermore, there is a report that temperature compensation of the ATPase activity of KaiC alone breaks down in the low-temperature range of 4–20 °C (Q~10~ = 1.39) [@itomiwa2026], which raises the intriguing question of how this relates to the clock's oscillation stopping at about 19 °C.

Next is the view that "the temperature-induced change in amplitude is itself part of temperature compensation," which corresponds to the "coupled strategy" of Section 9. Ruoff and colleagues argued that, for a temperature-compensated oscillator to keep the same period, it must traverse a larger orbit as temperature rises [@ruoff2003], and Kurosawa and colleagues likewise derived from mathematical models the relationship that the period cannot be kept constant unless the amplitude increases as temperature rises [@kurosawa2017]. In the KaiABC clock, Liu and colleagues' switch mechanism corresponds exactly to this, and the measured-value ledger estimated in Section 11 was also consistent with this type. Another mathematical model, which incorporates the coupling between structural changes of the KaiC hexamer and chemical reactions, also proposes a mechanism in which, as temperature rises, both amplitude and period increase so as to offset the acceleration of individual reactions [@sasai2022]. Furthermore, it has been argued that the temperature-dependent conformational change of KaiB itself (its fold switch) may be involved in temperature compensation [@zhang2024]. In metamorphic proteins such as KaiB, which interconvert between two different folds, one fold often partially unfolds at low temperature, and it has been suggested that this temperature sensitivity may function as an adaptation to environmental temperature [@liwang2025].

On the other hand, closer to the "division-of-labor strategy" are the views of François and colleagues and of Kidd and colleagues, also introduced in Section 9. In *Drosophila*, both the mean level and the amplitude of the oscillation of the clock protein TIM increase with temperature, with the amplitude roughly doubling between 18 and 29 °C. In doing so, the oscillation waveform and the phase differences with other clock factors barely change, and Kidd and colleagues interpret this as "evidence that a dedicated pathway responsible for temperature sensing is connected to a temperature-insensitive core oscillator" [@kidd2015]. That said, a study that reanalyzed the same experimental data points out that the waveform becomes more distorted at higher temperatures [@gibo2025].

These three views are not mutually exclusive. There is nothing strange about components temperature-compensated within a molecule, like the ATPase, coexisting in one and the same clock with components that affect both period and amplitude, like the KaiA–KaiB switch. Indeed, the two may even be different aspects of the same molecular process. According to Ito-Miwa and colleagues' preprint, within the KaiB–KaiC complex, KaiA promotes the exchange of ADP for ATP in KaiC's CI domain, which activates the CI-domain ATPase and promotes KaiB dissociation [@itomiwa2026]. In other words, "KaiA-mediated complex dissociation," which we named in Section 11 as a candidate for the "missing positive term," and "the nucleotide-binding state of the ATPase" may in fact be linked as one continuous molecular process. Looking at other organisms, in *Neurospora* the temperature-dependent change in clock-protein abundance has been proposed as the mechanism of phase shifts caused by temperature changes [@liu1998], and it has long been shown theoretically that a temperature-compensated mathematical model can become a damped oscillator at low temperature and entrain even to small temperature cycles of about 1 °C [@ruoff1996].

Of course, some questions have not yet been fully resolved. Fu and colleagues showed that temperature compensation through period-lengthening reactions works more readily in nonlinear regimes sufficiently far from a bifurcation point [@fu2024]. The in vitro KaiABC clock, on the other hand, appears, as we saw in Section 9, to operate relatively close to a Hopf bifurcation even in the physiological temperature range of 20–30 °C. That said, the fact that the squared amplitude changes almost in proportion to temperature does not by itself establish that the clock is so close to the bifurcation point that the mechanism of Fu and colleagues cannot operate, nor does their theory forbid compensation near a bifurcation point. How each reaction's control coefficient changes, and how the balance of the ledger shifts, as the bifurcation approaches is an issue that the simple model of this article cannot fully explain.

Finally, let us restate the limitations of the Rust model used in this article. The model does not explicitly include KaiC ATPase activity, the ring structure and intersubunit interactions of the hexamer, the conformational change of KaiB, or the bistability that Liu and colleagues demonstrated experimentally. The amplitude control coefficients depend strongly on the form of the sharp KaiA-sequestration switch (@eq-freeA), so the amplitude-ledger values calculated in this article are specific to this model. Likewise, the U → T reaction that played the role of temperature sensor in this article's division-of-labor strategy is merely a setting within this model. Moreover, in living cells, feedback loops via gene transcription and translation, and output systems that convey clock information to gene expression across the whole genome, are also closely coupled to this KaiABC core oscillator [@chavan2021]. Even so, the idea of "keeping ledgers" itself applies universally, independent of the model's details. By calculating the control coefficients for period, amplitude, and phase response and lining them up multiplied by each reaction's activation energy, we can compare, all on the same yardstick, which reactions keep the clock's pace and which sense temperature.

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

Finally, let us return to the three properties of circadian rhythms introduced in Section 1. "Temperature compensation," in which the period does not change when the ambient temperature changes, could be described as the balance of the period ledger (@eq-tc). The property of the clock stopping at low temperature was closely tied to the tilt of the "amplitude ledger" (@eq-dlnA), and "entrainment," which sets the clock's hands to a temperature cycle, to the "phase-response ledger" (@eq-gamma). In both the amplitude and phase-response ledgers, what essentially matters is the deviation of each reaction's activation energy from the mean, $E_i - \bar{E}$. Therefore, if the amplitude changes with temperature, the effect of temperature is not a mere uniform fast-forwarding; and if there were a clock in which all reactions had the same activation energy, it could never entrain to a temperature cycle, however sensitive to temperature it might be.

The main point this article has tried to convey is that "looking only at temperature compensation of the period, we cannot pin down the mechanism behind it." In theory there are countless combinations that bring the period ledger to zero, and as we saw in Sections 9 and 10, even with amplitude and phase response in view, it was hard to narrow the internal design of the model down to one from comparisons of macroscopic behavior alone. But by placing the control coefficients for period, amplitude, and phase response together with the temperature dependences measured for each reaction on the same ledger, we can concretely bring to light the processes missing from the current model and sharpen the hypotheses to test next.

Section 11 put this into practice. When the temperature dependences of individual reactions estimated from experiments were written into the ledger of the Rust model, the phosphorylation and dephosphorylation rates alone tipped the ledger strongly negative and could not reproduce temperature compensation. What was missing was "a large positive term on the period-lengthening side," and its sign matched exactly the properties of the process by which KaiA pulls apart the KaiB–KaiC complex—that is, the temperature-sensing switch mechanism. This becomes a hypothesis to be tested quantitatively with a mathematical model that explicitly incorporates the complex formation and dissociation switch. The question posed in Section 1 was, "Why is the clock as a whole insensitive to temperature when its components are sensitive to it?" From the ledger's point of view, these two are by no means contradictory: it suffices for temperature-sensitive components to cancel each other's effects on the ledger. And who the partners in that cancellation are can be sought out concretely by actually keeping the ledger.

The KaiABC clock, woven from just three proteins in a test tube, is a rare stage on which such deep questions about living systems can be pursued thoroughly in both the language of molecular structure and the language of mathematics. All the code used in this article is included on this page. Try swapping in other measured data or moving the temperature sensitivity to a different step, and keep your own "ledger."
